title: Structural Elucidation and Quantitative  Characterization of BDDE-Crosslinked Recombinant Human Type III Collagen by NMR Spectroscopy: Crosslinking Sites, Product Distribution,  and Enhanced Properties
content: Recombinant humanized collagen type III (rhCol III) has attracted growing interest as a biomaterial for tissue engineering, wound healing, and dermal fillers because of its excellent biocompatibility, low immunogenicity, and crucial role in tissue repair and regeneration. However, native rhCol III suffers from poor mechanical stability and rapid enzymatic degradation in vivo. Chemical crosslinking with 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether (BDDE) represents a well-established strategy to enhance the structural stability and application performance of collagen-based biomaterials. In this study, we present a comprehensive NMR spectroscopy investigation of BDDE-crosslinked rhCol III, combining one-dimensional (¹H and ¹³C) and two-dimensional (COSY, HSQC and HMBC) NMR experiments to definitively identify crosslinking sites, characterize reaction products, and quantify key crosslinking parameters. Using a recombinant type III collagen of approximately 55 kDa con-taining 18 lysine residues per molecule, we demonstrated that BDDE crosslinks collagen predominantly through covalent modification of the ε-amino groups of lysine residues under alkaline conditions. Quantitative NMR analysis determined key parameters including the degree of modi-fication (MoD), the crosslinker ratio (CrR), and the degree of crosslinking. Physicochemical characterization further showed that BDDE crosslinking markedly enhanced the thermal and mechanical stability of rhCol III, with the denaturation temperature increasing from 55.94 °C to 68.18 °C and the apparent viscosity improving by approximately 100-fold. Importantly, toxicity and safety as-sessment confirmed the biocompatibility of the crosslinked material. Collectively, these results establish a robust NMR-based characterization platform for BDDE-crosslinked collagen and demonstrate that the resulting biomaterial affords enhanced structural stability together with excellent biocompatibility, supporting its potential for tissue engineering and dermal filler applications.
